speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in accordance with the request made yesterday I should like to make a short statement on Canada's contribution to the Colombo plan.
A little over a year ago the foreign ministers of the commonwealth countries met in Colombo, Ceylon, to consider many of the urgent political and economic problems then facing Asia. Out of their discussions a consultative committee on south and southeast Asia was created which was charged with examining economic problems of the area and preparing appropriate recommendations. This committee, which drew its original membership from seven countries, the United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand, India, Pakistan, Ceylon and Canada, met in Sydney, Australia, last May and in London last September. Its most recent meeting in Colombo, Ceylon, ended yesterday.
The United States, with unanimous agreement of the seven original members, recently joined the consultative committee. In announcing his government's acceptance of this invitation, the Secretary of State in Washington said on January 24 of this year that it afforded his country the opportunity "for further co-operation with the countries of south and southeast Asia in their efforts toward economic and social development". Representatives of the following non-commonwealth countries also attended the recent meeting in Colombo: Burma, Cambodia, Viet Nam, Indonesia, the Philippines and Thailand.
During 1950, when the United States was continuing to carry such a heavy burden of foreign aid, it was, I think, appropriate that the commonwealth countries should examine together some of the pressing economic problems of south and southeast Asia. These were not new problems, but they were ones to which the free world had not previously given adequate attention. The commonwealth countries did good work, therefore, in bringing together in one report an analysis of the needs of the countries which comprise four-fifths of the area of south and southeast Asia.
Since the plan was drawn up, there have already been significant economic changes which are bound to affect its progress, at least in its initial stages. The burden of rearmament which the western countries have been forced to take on is having major economic consequences. The prices of many of the raw materials produced in south and southeast Asia have gone up sharply. This advantage to producers in the area has been offset to some extent by the rising cost of the goods which the Asian countries must import. Even more serious are the difficulties in obtaining delivery of critically needed goods. Most regrettable, there has been a serious falling off in India's food supply owing to drought in some regions, floods in others and locusts in still others. This has imposed a very real human and economic problem upon India.
The Colombo plan calls for a capital development program in commonwealth countries of south and southeast Asia totalling about $5 billion over a six-year period starting this year. Of this $5 billion it is expected that about $2 billion will be raised internally and about $3 billion will come from external sources. Private capital is one source, though in the present international situation it cannot be as important as it should be. We also hope that the international bank will be another source for financing some of the larger projects. So far as government contributions are concerned, the United Kingdom has announced that its contribution over the six-year period will take the form of sterling balance releases, at a high and fixed rate, grants for colonial development, and loans floated in London, amounting to well over 300 million pounds sterling, or more than 900 million Canadian dollars for the six years. Australia has announced that it will provide 7 million pounds sterling, which is nearly 21 million Canadian dollars in the first year, and that over the six-year period its contribution will be not less than 25 million pounds sterling, that is nearly 75 million Canadian dollars.
The Canadian government has been giving very serious consideration to the course of action which should be recommended to parliament. We have been conscious that Canadians, as individuals-and this has been clearly reflected in the press from one end

The Colombo Plan
of the country to the other-wish to contribute to the success of this plan. This desire of the people of Canada to extend assistance has also been clearly shown in the debate on the speech from the throne. It was reflected by the remarks of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) when he expressed his confidence that members of the house would support all practical measures which will bring hope and encouragement to those who are in such great distress in so many parts of the world. It was reflected also in the remarks of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cold-well), when he called the Colombo plan the most imaginative ever adopted by the commonwealth countries.
The government therefore authorized Mr. David Johnson, our high commissioner in Pakistan and our delegate to the recent meeting of the consultative committee, to state that the Canadian government would ask parliament to appropriate $25 million as its contribution to the first year of the plan, provided it was clear that other contributing countries would be making appropriate contributions so that the broad objectives of the Colombo plan might be realized.
The United States representative at the Colombo meeting said that his government welcomed the initiative of the countries participating in the Colombo plan; that the plan itself appeared to offer a basis for genuine economic progress, and that the United States intended to co-ordinate to the greatest extent possible the program it had undertaken or might undertake in the area with those programs under the Colombo plan.
I should also inform the house that we are immediately opening discussions with the Indian government to see whether they would wish that some of the funds we provide this year under the Colombo plan should be spent on Canadian wheat for their famine-stricken country. As yet we do not know exactly what types of wheat, available in Canada, will be of use to India; nor, of course, do we know what next year's crop will be. However, it is our hope that some wheat may be provided to the government of India in connection with the plan. This wheat, I imagine, would be sold by the Indian government to the people of India under its rationing system, where possible, and the money so raised could then be devoted to capital developments. In the Colombo report it is clearly recognized, especially in the case of India, that imports of food as well as imports of capital goods may serve in attaining the objectives of the plan. At the same time that we open discussions

with the Indian authorities we shall open parallel discussions with the Pakistan authorities.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, perhaps I might read to the house the last sentence of the Colombo report, which summarizes so eloquently our hopes for the success of the Colombo plan:
In a world racked by schism and confusion it is doubtful whether free men can long afford to leave undeveloped and imprisoned in poverty the human resources of the countries of south and southeast Asia which could help so greatly, not only to restore the world's prosperity, but also to redress its confusion and enrich the lives of all men everywhere.
If I may ask the minister a short question, do I understand that our contribution is not contingent upon a substantial financial contribution by the United States?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Well, Mr. Speaker, I do not want to begin a discussion of this matter at this time. In reply to the hon. gentleman I would merely say that to carry out the original plan in its entirety, a contribution from the United States will be essential. The contribution we shall ask parliament to make is not in a sense conditional upon anything; but if the plan could not be carried out in its entirety, naturally we would have to re-examine the whole position.
May I ask the minister-

Order. The minister has stated that he will ask parliament to approve the contribution of this sum of money. In the circumstances I think questions should be withheld until that legislation is brought down.

Under the London agreement of March, 1945, the United Kingdom, United States, France, and the U.S.S.R. set up a special international military tribunal (which later sat at Nuremberg) to deal with major war crimes. 1.	Does the federal government recognize any organizations of its employees as bargaining agents in the terms or spirit of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act?
2.	What steps are being taken by the government to provide its employees with the same facilities for negotiation with respect to working conditions as are provided for the employees of private corporations under the terms of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act?
3.	Are any labour-management committees operating in government departments?
4.	If so (a) how many; (b) in what departments, or sections or branches are such committees operating?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
1.	The answer to the question as drafted is no.
The civil service of Canada is carried on under laws enacted by parliament and is supervised by a commission set up by parliament and which reports to parliament. The commission and the government can and do receive representations from organizations of employees, but there is no process of collective bargaining in the sense in which that term is used in industry.
From the very nature of employment in the public service, there can be no bargaining agent for the nation comparable with the employer in industry who has at his disposal funds derived from payments for goods or services. The funds from which salaries are paid in the public service have to be voted by parliament and parliament alone can discharge that responsibility.
2.	The answer is that no steps are being taken because it is considered that the appropriate machinery for these purposes was set up by P.C. 3676 of May 16, 1944 which established the national joint council of the public service of Canada and the subsequent treasury board minute of March 8, 1945, approving the constitution of the council.
3	and 4. There is nothing which could properly be called a labour-management committee, but there is a departmental joint

council of the public service in the Department of Resources and Development and there are numerous staff associations in other departments who are concerned with and make representations on working conditions and welfare questions.

PROPOSAL TO GIVE CLEAR TITLES TO VETERANS WITH UNPAID BALANCES
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into consideration the advisability of giving clear titles to all soldier settlers of great war I who hold land under contract with the soldier settlement board.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the resolution standing in my name on the order paper, for possibly the sixteenth time in the past number of years, is one with which all members are familiar. On many occasions since coming to this house I have heard members of the government say that Canada will always honour her obligations. I have no argument whatever with that principle, and it has been carried out with perhaps a few exceptions, one of them in connection with the soldier settlers of world war I. A promise was made by the then prime minister of Canada, the late Sir Robert Borden, that certain things would be done for those men after they returned from overseas. This is the speech that was given to those men back in 1917:
You are men actually facing the enemy day and night. You are suffering greatly from fatigue, overstrain, and lack of rest. The marvel of it is that men could undergo such a strain without breaking: but you have never yet broken, and history will appreciate that in days to come.
You men are about to enter one of the most serious engagements that ever faced the Canadian corps. I cannot, at this moment, give any information as to where this attack will be staged, whether it will be successful or not ... it is to be borne in mind that it will not be an easy success . . . We feel confident that you will succeed where others failed: for you have never yet failed in anything you have set your hand to, as a Canadian corps.
You can go into this action feeling assured of this, and as the head of the government, I give you this assurance: that you need have no fear that the government and the country will fail to show just

appreciation of your service to the country and empire in what you are about to do and what you have already done.
The government and the country will consider it their first duty to see that a proper appreciation of your effort and of your courage is brought to the notice of the people at home, and it will always be our endeavour to so guide the attitude of public opinion, that the country will support the government to prove to the returned man its just and due appreciation of the inestimable value of the services rendered to the country and empire; and that no man, whether he goes back or whether he remains in Flanders, will have just cause to reproach the government for having broken faith with the men who won and the men who died.
Mr. Speaker, I have read this into the record many times before, because I believe it is always necessary to have something on which to base your case. I believe we have sound grounds upon which to base our case, for giving clear title to the veterans of world war I who settled under the soldier settlement board. After the war these soldiers returned, and I understand that many of them congregated in the cities where there was no employment for them. The government of the day deemed it necessary to provide some of them with farms as a means of solving a portion of the unemployment across the country. As a result of that decision, legislation was passed in 1919 making provision for such loans to be advanced to these men as would enable them to buy farms.
As has been pointed out on several occasions, the move was one without precedence. It was a hastily improvised scheme, and was put into operation by men who had had no previous experience in that line. I am sorry to say that it caused a lot of unnecessary suffering and hardship to the men who made use of it. It may seem strange to us, but before any contracts were signed by those men the legislation provided that in any case where oil rights went with the land, those rights were to be taken away because the men were farmers and not miners or oil operators. In effect, to take away the right to the oil which was under the land amounted to the same thing as taking away buildings that were on the land. I feel that an injustice was done through that provision, which I believe was section 57 of the act.
In 1938 an attempt was made by this house to have those rights restored to the men to whom they properly belonged. The House of Commons, with very little discussion, passed legislation to that end, and it was sent on to the upper house. Some of the members up there who were not farmers thought it desirable to have the legislation sent to a committee. This committee reported that the legislation should be disallowed, and that was done. Thanks to the former 80709-35
Soldier Settlers
minister of veterans affairs, who is now the' Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg), those rights have been restored to the veterans, and at least a part of the injustice has been removed.
As a result of the soldier settler legislation of 1919, some 25,017 veterans were settled on the land. They were given loans averaging $4,358.40 each, which came to a total amount of $109,034,331. The interest rate to begin with was far too high, particularly as applied to men who had gone overseas to fight our battles for us. Had it not been for their service, perhaps we would not be in control of that land today. The rate of interest set out in the bill was five per cent on current accounts. When it came to the time that the men could not make their payments, the interest rate was stepped up to seven per cent on arrears. We might compare that figure with the interest rate charged to veterans of the second world war, when provision was made for an interest rate of 3J per cent. Personally, I feel, as I have felt right along, that that interest rate is too high.
When these contracts were drawn up, it is not surprising to find that there was a stated sum to be paid by the settlers. In many cases they were charged far too much for their land, their livestock and their farm implements. Yet in spite of this fact, no provision was made for a guaranteed price for the products they grew or the stock they raised. At the time many of those contracts were entered into, wheat was selling at as high as $3 a bushel, and in some cases a little more; but before many years had passed, the price had slipped back to twenty cents a bushel. For milch cows, which most settlers had to have, they paid anywhere from $125 to $150 apiece; yet not many years later the price of those cows had dropped to anywhere from $10 to $15 per head. The settler paid $500 a team, and sometimes more, for horses that were aged and should have been turned out to pasture as being useless; within not many years they were selling for $50 or $60 per team. But in spite of this reduction in the price of the things the settler had to sell, the contract price still held good, and it was impossible for those men to make a living and to pay their debts. Realizing the impossible position these men were in, the government finally decided that they would reduce the amount of the original debt. Later, when that was found not to be enough, there was a cancellation of some of the interest. But in spite of that, during the years following 1929, when a man-made recession was brought about, the men continued to slip back and their debts continued

Soldier Settlers
to pile up. There was therefore not much advantage to be gained by these reductions and cancellations.
About 1934 or 1935 legislation was passed providing for a dollar-for-dollar concession on the payment of arrears. That would have been fine if everybody had had money. But everybody did not have money. In fact few had any money with which to take advantage of that offer; and by 1938 that legislation was discontinued. In 1939 we were still in the depression, and with 1939 came world war II. Many of those old soldier settlers who had been through the mud, the dirt and the suffering of the first war, because of their financial and economic conditions enlisted again in world war II; and many of them took their sons with them. The men who were left at home were those who were unable to go; and they got busy on the land, worked long hours and continued to produce food for Canadians and some for shipment overseas. Many of them also went to the munitions factories and, where their health permitted them to do so, worked until the end of the war. During that time there was shameful treatment of the families remaining on the land, of the men who had gone overseas or had enlisted in the services.
I have here a copy of sessional paper 194A, P.C. 138/1936, certified to be a true copy of a minute of a meeting of the treasury board, approved by His Excellency the Governor General in council on the 19th March, 1941. This is an order in council that provided that the soldier settlement board should collect its pound of flesh from the family of the veteran, even though he was overseas and fighting in the second world war. Under the heading "Soldier Settlement" the order in council reads as follows:
The board has had under consideration a submission of the Honourable the Minister of Mines and Resources reporting that:
Let me state here, Mr. Speaker, that that minister of mines and resources was none other than Hon. T. A. Crerar, who for some time had under his administration the soldier settlement board legislation; and it would appear that he turned that administration over to Mr. Gordon Murchison, the director -I was going to say the dictator. Perhaps if I leave the two word's in, it might be all right. But apparently Mr. Murchison was allowed to go on without any ministerial supervision and to impose his will upon the settlers. The order in council continues:
1. A considerable number of persons who agreed to purchase farms from the soldier settlement board or from the director of soldier settlement on long term contracts have enlisted in the Canadian armed forces.

2.	In many cases the dependents of such enlisted persons continue to occupy their farms but no provision has been made for payment of instalments in respect of their contracts or of taxes in respect of their farms.
3.	The director of soldier settlement has no authority to carry such accounts indefinitely and it is considered desirable to provide for deduction from dependents1' allowances to cover local taxes and interest due.
Accordingly the board recommend that notwithstanding any provision to the contrary contained in any of the regulations providing for payment of dependents' or marriage allowances in respect of dependents of members of the Canadian armed forces, in all cases where the dependents of an enlisted person continue to occupy the farm for which such person is indebted to the director of soldier settlement and in respect of which the contract terms are not otherwise satisfactorily provided for, there may be deducted from the dependents' or marriage allowance amounts sufficient to provide for payment of taxes levied by the local taxing authority in respect of the property in question and interest accruing annually on indebtedness to the director of soldier settlement, such deductions to be made monthly and in no case to exceed $20 per month except with the consent of the dependents concerned.
That, Mr. Speaker, is one of the most shameful pieces of legislation by order in council that has been enacted in a long time. It did not matter whether the wives and children of the veteran who had gone away for the second time had enough to eat or not; the director of soldier settlement, Mr. Gordon Murchison, had to have his interest accounts and his taxes taken care of. As soon as we found out that some suffering had been caused the settlers-because a great deal of suffering was being endured by many veterans all across the country-that was taken care of and done away with.
I might say that since 1937 I have been interested in this matter because right around the neighbourhood where I farmed for many years we had a number of these soldier settlers. I personally know that prices which were twice what they should have been were charged for land, livestock and equipment. In a short time there was a general demand that a clear title be given to all veterans holding land under the soldier settlement board.
In 1937 an organization was set up at Lloydminster that did quite a little work along that line, and later another organization came into existence in the city of Saskatoon, which carried on from there, known as the Soldier Settlers Association of Canada. It did a lot of work. We had several discussions in the house here in connection with their program; and they also caused a petition to be circulated, which was signed by over 12,500 people who could be reached at that time of the year, because the ground

was all covered with snow, travel was practically impossible, and no provision was made for paying the persons who carried those petitions.
The request was also supported by the Alberta legislature, the Saskatchewan legislature, the Alberta Farmers' Union, the Saskatchewan Association of Rural Municipalities, the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, the United Farmers of Canada, Saskatchewan section; the United Farmers of Alberta, the Alberta branch of the Canadian Legion, the executive of the British Columbia branch of the Canadian Legion, and many others across the country.
In addition to that we had a brief presented to the veterans committee here in the house on October 26, 1945. Mr. Alex Walker, president of the Canadian Legion at that time, was the spokesman. A part of the brief, under the heading: "Soldier Settlement Act," reads as follows:
A further proposal recommended by this committee relates to the granting of clear titles to aged settlers or to those who had reduced their indebtedness to twenty-five per cent of the original purchase price. A great deal of discussion has been carried on during the past few years respecting soldier settlers of the last war, and strong representations, from time to time, have been made from various sources to solve the problem of these veterans by granting them clear title to their farms. A debate occurred in the House of Commons recently on this subject and many members spoke in favour of the proposal. Representations by soldier settlers through the Legion have followed similar lines, and the following resolution is submitted for the consideration of this committee:
The resolution reads:
Therefore be it resolved that, in order to be fair to our aging veterans and to bring the old and the new settlement acts more into line, the dominion government be asked to readjust the debts of the 6,153 original soldier settlers who have not paid for their lands, such readjustment to take into consideration the difference in interest rates charged under the said acts; and that following such readjustment the government be further asked to cancel the debts of those original soldier settlers whose debt has been, or may hereafter be, reduced to twenty-five per cent of the original purchase price or the reduced purchase price.
In dealing with the interest rates charged, Mr. Speaker, I believe that if the old settlers had been charged 3$ per cent instead of 5 per cent or 7 per cent, there would not be a dollar of debt remaining in most of the cases at this time.
After the brief was presented there were questions and answers, as indicated on page 315 of the report for the day on which the brief was presented. We find the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) asking this question:
On page 11 of the brief there is a reference to the old soldier settlers, and the recommendation there is that clear title be given provided a soldier reduces his indebtedness to twenty-five per cent of the original purchase price or the reduced purchase 80709-35 i
Soldier Settlers
price. I do not think that will go far enough to satisfy the organization that calls itself the Old Soldier Settlers Organization, because they are asking for a clear title for all soldier settlers of the last war. I think we must all agree that the soldiers who are in the most difficult position of all are those soldier settlers who have had no chance of reducing their indebtedness to that twenty-five per cent, the ones who have been up against bad luck. Some of you may call it bad management perhaps, but we know that the situation these men went through in the depression years put them in a position where they could not get the money to buy the farm. I should like very much to see that twenty-five per cent taken out of your recommendation, making it wide open so that title can be given to the old soldier settlers, whether in the fortunate position of being able to reduce their indebtedness to twenty-five per cent or not. I wonder if Mr. Walker would comment on that?
And the witness, who was Mr. Walker, said:
I am sure it will not hurt our feelings if you do give them clear title.
That was the president of the Canadian Legion, speaking for that organization.
Coming back to the soldier settlement organization, we had them here on the 17th of June, 1948, and they presented their final brief on that day. The committee did not consider the brief on that day, but at a subsequent meeting they did consider it, and this is the report that they presented to the house later on, under the heading:	"Soldier
Settlement Act":
Your committee recommends that all indebtedness of soldier settlers under the provisions of the Soldier Settlement Act, 1918. be remitted, and that they may be granted clear title to their holdings.
That was the position taken by the veterans committee, one of the best committees that was ever set up in this house. There were representatives of all parties on that committee. They did not get down to the tactics that perhaps some of the other committees had been using, namely, trying to get political advantage in that committee. Therefore we should at least take notice of the veterans committee of the house and the brief presented by the Canadian Legion.
Some causes of failure of the settlers may be enumerated. We find that many of them were unsuited for farming, and might be classed as square pegs in round holes. Had they been placed in some other walk of life they would have come out very well. We know that in the house we have square pegs in round holes also; and yet people must be fitted to some line of work which they are able to do. Moreover, land, livestock and implements were purchased at inflated prices. Land was purchased in some instances in dry areas or in areas subject to frost and hail. The prices of agricultural products, as I have already said, went to low levels; in the case of wheat, running anywhere from $3

Soldier Settlers
down to $0.20 a bushel, and the price of other commodities in line with that. Then the interest rates ran from five to seven per cent a year. They became too high. That put a number of these men in difficulties and kept them there, because after paying five per cent or seven per cent interest on arrears, which took a large part of their profit, they found that they were still no further ahead than they were one year prior to that time.
We have made loans to other countries sometimes interest free, and sometimes at as low as two per cent; only this afternoon the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) told us about this country giving a grant of $25 million to support the Colombo plan during the first year of operation. It might be well if some of these things were given to take care of our veterans at home.
Titles should be granted because the scheme, as it was admitted by Mr. Crerar, who was minister of mines and resources at the time, was hastily improvised and put into operation or administered by people who had no previous experience. It was intended as a rehabilitation scheme to fit many of the veterans. It has turned out to be a scheme of persecution.
The average age of the settlers at the present time runs over sixty years. Some of these veterans are now nearly ninety, and if they have not been able to pay off their debts up to the present time, how in the world does the government expect them to pay off their debts in the future? Those who have paid off or will pay off in the future have been denying themselves many of the comforts of life. They have been living in shacks that are not good enough, certainly for our veterans, and they have been denying themselves the advantage of medical, dental, hospital and other care, to which they are justly entitled.
In some instances the old settlers went overseas-sent their sons or took them with them. Many of them, as I said before, went to the munitions factories and continued to help out there.
Lastly, while the settlers were bound by contract to pay back a certain amount in return for their land, no provision whatever was made for keeping the prices of their products up to the point at which they should have been kept. That was the faulty agricultural policy pursued by the government.
While there have been many discussions of this matter in the house, the only effective objection I have ever heard is that if the veterans of great war I are given clear title, then the veterans of great war II will demand

the same treatment. I do not think that objection is a sound one, and I shall deal with it later.
In 1949 there were 911 settlers who paid in $697,921.98. During that calendar year there were 692 reductions, amounting in all to $269,311.95. In 1950 we note quite a reduction in the number of settlers whose accounts were fully paid up; it dropped from 911 in 1949 to 362 in 1950. The 362 paid in $410,233.76. In 1950 there were 226 reductions made, as compared with the 692 of the previous year; and those 226 reductions amounted to $106,386.34. This amount includes 25 reductions amounting to $13,493.22, authorized before January 21, 1950, which might properly have been included in the 1949 figure.
The average debt of the settlers on January 1, 1950, was $1,125.03, whereas the average debt on January 1, 1951, was $1,122.73. Last year's estimates made provision for the sum of $150,000 to reduce this debt still further. We find that up until the end of December $106,386 had been spent; that would be during'the first nine months of the last fiscal year. On January 1 of this year there were 1,272 of these settlers who were still in debt.
The total debt as of January 1, 1951 amounted to $1,428,069.42. Looking back we remember that the daily cost of fighting the second world war was approximately $16 million. If at this time we were to apply the cost of fighting only two and one-half hours of that war, title could be given to all those old settlers. The over-all cost of world war II now runs to more than $21 billion. The interest on the national debt runs to over $450 million; and while many people say, "Give the old veterans something for nothing", we find in this interest on the debt a good example of something for nothing, because much of that debt on which we are paying interest is nothing more than figures in bankers' books. We feel it should not be in that position.
There are fourteen million people in Canada. With the debt of these old settlers standing at $1,428,069.42 we realize that if every individual in Canada paid one dime, one ten-cent piece, the price of a chocolate bar, in addition to his or her other taxes-which, I realize, will be heavy enough-this debt could) be wiped out altogether.
In conclusion, let me say that Canada is the best country in the world, and I fear no successful contradiction' of that statement. I believe this country has provided a great deal for the veterans who returned from the second world war; and credit for that cannot

be claimed by any one political party, because we know that parties on all sides of the house worked together to bring about good deals for the returned men. I do not believe the treatment they are getting in that respect is any more than they should be getting. They offered everything they had in order to win the war; and they did win it, gloriously.
We should see that those old veterans who settled on the land after the first great war should be given simple justice, even at this late date. Last year's frozen crops were enough to discourage many farmers, even those who are in good financial standing. But what is the effect upon those old veterans when they look at their pile of debt? Let us not forget that they owe money to people other than the soldier settlement board. Their crops in many instances are lying under the snow today, and it remains to 'be seen whether they will reap any benefit from those crops.
They have been paying on their land for the past thirty-one years and have denied themselves and their families much needed medical attention. In many cases their machinery is worn out, and their buildings are badly depreciated. They are faced with excessive costs of the things they have to buy, and diminishing returns for the things they have to sell. Perhaps, if conditions do not change, in the very near future, we may need1 the help of those men and their families again to provide food and munitions of war for Canadians and for people overseas. Today we should make them happy and give them title to their lands, because it may be later than you think. I hope it will not be necessary for me to discuss this matter again. I wish to pay tribute to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg), the former minister of veterans affairs, who has been most sympathetic and helpful. I pay tribute also to the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Mutch), his parliamentary assistant, who, too, has been helpful, and who was one of the first members on the government side of the house to come out openly in support of clear titles as a matter of good business, not just from a sympathetic standpoint. I have not yet had any dealings in connection with this matter with the new Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe) but I look forward to sympathetic treatment from him of those soldier settlers of the first great war.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO GIVE CLEAR TITLES TO VETERANS WITH UNPAID BALANCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
the subject under discussion this afternoon is not a new one. As the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) has said, it has been before the house on many occasions.
Soldier Settlers
This resolution, innocent in appearance, reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into consideration the advisability of giving clear titles to all soldier settlers of great war I who hold land under contract with the soldier settlement board.
This resolution simply asks the government to take into consideration the advisability of taking action, and I am satisfied that it will have the support of all members in the house, no matter where they sit. I commend and congratulate the hon. member who has just taken his seat upon his consistency in bringing this matter to the attention of the house over a long period of years. He deserves credit not only from members of the house but more particularly from those whose cause he has been pleading.
I have also spoken in the matter. As every veteran in the house knows, the matter has been before the veterans committee on numerous occasions, and has been recommended by the Canadian Legion to that committee. The history of the matter has been pretty thoroughly covered. The hon. member who introduced the resolution has placed statistics on record and has summed up the situation over the last thirty years, since the inception of the act.
Those of us who served in the first great war will remember the time when the young men came back from overseas in 1918 and 1919. These young men came back with high hopes. The hon. member cited the promise made to them by the then prime minister of Canada, and of course they had reason to believe that they would be well looked after. In 1919, when the act first came into force, 25,000 men took up land under the Soldier Settlement Act. At that time the amount involved was in the vicinity of $110 million. That was to be the cost to the 25,000 soldiers.
We find that in 1951 the figure of 25,000 soldiers, who owed for their farms at that time, has been reduced to 1,272 according to a return brought down the other day. Practically all these men have paid for their farms, and of the remaining 1,272 some of them have paid most of their indebtedness. At the present time the amount owed by these men is only $1,428,000. I am sure that all hon. members will agree that is a very small sum indeed when we consider the millions and billions of dollars this country has to pay in a year in order to carry on our services. From 1919 to 1951 these men have indeed had a long, long trail to travel. It has been a hard and stony road. I think we could very well give every consideration tr

Soldier Settlers
the resolution, and I hope that when the minister speaks he will be able to tell the house that there will be an item in the estimates this year to deal with this matter.
As I said a moment ago, most of these men have paid for their farms over the years, and I think those who have not paid have in many cases had good reason for not paying. They were handicapped in many ways. Many of them had poor farms to start with. I think that is a fact, and it is not surprising because out of 25,000 farms there is every reason to expect that some of them would be poor and would be farms on which a man could not make a living. Besides poor farms these men had hard luck. They took up farming almost at the very worst time in the history of this country. They were farming during the poor years of the twenties, during the depression of the thirties, and after that another war commenced. Therefore they did not have a fair opportunity to pay for their farms. Some of these men had large families and found it most difficult, as the hon. member who has just taken his seat said, to look after their families during hard times.
They paid high prices not only for their farms but also for their stock and machinery. The price of stock at that time might not compare with the price of cattle today but $100 or $150 for a cow in 1919 or 1920 was a very high price for those times, and many of these men had to pay such prices. They also had to pay a high price for their farm machinery. In the second great war the government had the benefit of their experience with these men, and I think that was worth a great deal not only to the Department of Veterans Affairs but also to the government generally. They might very well take that factor into consideration when a request is made for the cancelling of the debts on these farms.
We might say that the men of the first war were more or less guinea pigs so far as these farms were concerned, and that in the second great war the experience which the government had gained was of most valuable assistance and no doubt saved the people of Canada many millions of dollars. Again, it was difficult for these men to sell at times when the prices of farm products were at their peak. In my own province many of these men were potato farmers. The agent of the soldier settlement board would come around and say: You must sell your potatoes now. You owe the department so much money. The man would say:	If you will
allow me to sell in a month or two months' time I will be able to sell at a better price than if I sell now. But the agent was doing

his duty. He was always anxious to see that the men paid when payment was due. Therefore in many cases men were forced to sell their potatoes, pigs, apples, or whatever it was, at a time when they could not get the best market price.
The hon. member said that these men have made other contributions besides the payments they have made. As I mentioned before, most of them were men who raised large families. In the second great war sons and daughters of these returned soldiers went overseas to serve. Hundreds of these men served in the veterans guard or in some other branch of the services during world war II. Taking all these matters into consideration, here we have men who have worked on these farms for over thirty years. Today they are between sixty and seventy-five years of age. At this time, when it is practically impossible for them to work on account of their age and it is becoming practically impossible for them to pay for their farms, they are asking the government to give them title so that in their old age they may at least be able to say that they own the land on which they have reared their families and on which they have lived for so long.
I do not think that such action would establish a precedent so far as world war II veterans are concerned. We all know that the veterans of the second world war received about one-third or 33 per cent equity in their land to start with. We also know that, instead of paying 5 per cent as was paid by the veterans of the first world war, they are only paying 3i per cent. I might add, as has already been stated, that in 1942, I believe it was, the interest rate was reduced from 5 per cent to 3J per cent for veterans who had joined the veterans guard or some other branch of the services, and for those who had not gone overseas it was made 3| per cent in 1944.
In changing this contract or agreement, as I say we would not be establishing a precedent. Already that contract has been changed several times, first in regard to the rate of interest and then in the matter of reductions. Several substantial reductions have been made at various times, and I believe the former minister and his predecessor deserve a great deal of credit in that connection. A precedent was also established in regard to the time these men were given in which to pay for their farms. At first it was twenty-five years; then along about 1945 that period was extended for another twenty years, making forty-five years in all. So we have several precedents for making changes in these agreements, and no objection could be taken if we made another change.

I am not going to make any extended remarks on this subject, but it does seem to me that after all these years, considering the men with whom we are dealing, considering the toil, suffering and hard work they have put in, it would not be becoming on the part of the government to stick to logic and statistics. There is always a time when we should let a little sentiment enter into our considerations, and I think this is that time. We have an opportunity to make those old men very happy. I am sure we will not only make the veterans who own these farms happy; we will also make the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) very happy. For fifteen years he has been fighting this cause, and I would like to see him win. He has been a great fighter, and the soldiers owe him a great debt.
I do not think we would lose so much as far as money is concerned. I remember that a few years ago some hon. member figured out what it cost to carry on debates here in the House of Commons, and it ran to thousands of dollars a day. If we could turn into money the time that has been taken by the hon. member for Battle River and the rest of us in discussing this matter, I am sure it would amount to a very substantial portion of this indebtedness. There is also the cost of administration. I know the soldier settlement board is no longer in existence and that this matter is administered under the Veterans Land Act, but even so I am quite satisfied that it costs a good deal of money each year to administer the land held by these soldier settlers. Taking all these things into consideration I am quite sure it would take only a few years to make up this whole amount, if today, or as soon as it could be done, we gave these men clear title to the land on which they live. The amount involved is only $1,428,000. A few years ago I remember hearing a minister ask, "Why, what is a million dollars?" With the billions of dollars being expended by this country every year; with the hundreds of millions it takes to carry on even our ordinary services, a million dollars is a very small amount indeed.
Without discussing the matter further, I feel that a very strong case has been made out for these veterans of the first war who are on these farms. I believe this resolution should have the support and commendation of all hon. members, and I am sure that people from one end of Canada to the other, whether veterans or not, will feel that we are only giving simple justice to a body of men who have deserved it for a long period of years.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO GIVE CLEAR TITLES TO VETERANS WITH UNPAID BALANCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope I will not take quite as long
Soldier Settlers
as the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks), since we have heard how much it costs when we speak in this house. I would rather have my money go toward paying off one of these mortgages. I want to congratulate the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair).
I sincerely hope the rest of his party will not be here as long as I am going to be here, but if he does not win out this year I hope he comes back to continue the fight. On behalf of every soldier settler in my riding, and I think every veteran, I congratulate him on the stand he has taken and wish him success.
There are only 1,272 veterans concerned in this, so I do not think anyone can accuse any hon. member of speaking from a political angle. If you scatter 1,272 veterans across the ten provinces of Canada I am sure their vote would not affect any hon. member. But there is such a thing as justice tempered with mercy, and I believe this is the place for it. The only argument I have heard against this proposal is that it would be unfair to those who have paid for their land. Well, I can say with all sincerity that no soldier settler in my riding who has paid his debt will begrudge these men anything they get, nor do I think any veteran in Canada will begrudge them anything.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to support this resolution sponsored by the member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) which reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into consideration the advisability of giving clear titles to all soldier settlers of great war I who hold land under contract with the soldier settlement board.
It is rather difficult to say something about this subject that is not a repetition of what other members have said. This is not a political matter. Everyone has sympathy for the soldier settlers. I should like to pay tribute to the member for Battle River for his persistence in bringing this subject to the attention of the house year after year, and to the progress that he has made in getting some concessions. I believe it was in 1948 that a similar resolution was considered by the war veterans committee and recommended to the house. The veterans committee recommended that the soldiers be given clear title. This government did not grant that request but did go some distance towards

it at that time. I believe a lot of the credit for that should go to the member for Battle River.
I do not rise at this time merely because I belong to the Legion or because I am an oldi soldier; I rise as a Canadian. Most of these settlers went farming just about the same time as I did, in 1920. I know the hardships I encountered, and I suppose they met some of those hardships too. Perhaps they were less able to stand the knocks than I have been. We started out with wheat at $2.50, and everything that you touched or thought about was based on $2.50 wheat. If you bought a team of horses, they were based on the price of wheat. If you bought a farm, it was based on the price of wheat. Within two years the cows for which we paid $150 each were worth about $25 each. The member for Battle River referred to the price of a team of horses as $500. In about two years' time you could not get $100 for them. Those things all worked hardship on the soldier settler. The machinery he had to buy was high priced. He did not pay cash for that machinery, but he bought it on time. He bought his horses and everything else on time. He had to pay through the nose for those things during the remaining years.
Some remarks have been passed to the effect that the settlers who have been more fortunate, and who have paid their indebtedness to the board, would object if effect were given to this resolution. I do not think they would;. Nobody would object to this. Most of these men are sixty or over, and they have helped build Canada. Many of them gave their sons in the second world war, and no doubt if they struggle along a while longer they will see their grandsons going away to another war. I want to assure the government that every member in this group is behind this resolution. We appeal to the government to give these soldier settlers a clear title. They deserve it. They have paid for it. The greater portion of what they owe today is compound interest at seven per cent. That was a terrible toll on a man struggling for existence, especially in the thirties, when he started out on the basis of $2.50 wheat only to find that wheat dropped to 35 cents a bushel, barley to 15 cents, and oats to 5 cents. These men were the victims of circumstances. I again appeal to the government to give them clear title, and let them hold their heads high for the few remaining years in which they will be here.

I know of one settler who was settled on a very poor half section. He had agreed to pay about $17 an acre, in all about $5,500. Through no fault of his own, in the hungry and difficult thirties, he was advised by the inspector to sign a quit-claim deed. This he did. This fellow was rather a livestock man and he wanted to buy the same farm for pasture purposes. Owing to the regulations the board refused to sell this farm back to the same settler who had signed the quitclaim deed. On the other hand, they sold this half section to a speculator, who is not even a British subject, for less than $1 an acre. That is a concrete example of something that happened during that time under the soldier settlement board. When I think of things like that, I cannot understand why they should be niggardly or sticking with regard to granting free titles to these people who have spent the greater part of their lives on these farms.
I also want to endorse what the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) has said about this matter of oil or the mineral rights to properties. I had a somewhat similar case brought to my attention the other day. It is true enough that you can make a search in the titles office for fifty cents. But I had a letter back stating that they could not give me the information I wanted and that I would have to have a proper legal search made. That is the point which my good friend the hon. member for Fraser Valley was covering. You require to put up $25 for a legal search. I have knowledge of far worse cases than that. I will admit it is a matter of red tape. I am not blaming the present Veterans Land Act administration for it. But not all the oil in Canada is located in Alberta. Oil has been struck to some extent at least in Manitoba just west of Virden. The irony of the situation is that this oil has been struck on the property of a veteran of the last war, by the name of Rogers. He was overseas during the last war and while he was away his father purchased for him a farm on which the government retained the mineral rights or the oil

rights. Because the young lad did not purchase it through the V.L.A. administration, he is not now able to obtain these oil rights on the property on which they have struck oil. As I say, I realize that it is a matter of red tape through the V.L.A. But if a man can prove that he has rendered service the same as any man who has gone through V.L.A. and has purchased his property, surely he should be granted the oil rights to the piece of property. I think that is only fair and just. I think this is a case of great hardship. Some members have mentioned the conditions under which they were settled there. I remember quite well the Winnipeg strike being on in the latter part of 1919, and trainloads of soldiers being sent out from the city of Winnipeg to the area in which 1 settled, being taken down and shown certain areas of land there, in order to try to get them away from Winnipeg just for a week or ten days until the trouble there was over. Many of these young men took land in that area, although they had no farming experience. But promises were made to them; offers were made to them; and they accepted those offers. But in a short time they found that conditions were such that they just could not fulfil their commitments under the act. As to the small numbers that are left today -some 1,272 settlers-I know that in my own area they are cases of hardship, in practically every instance: there has been a large family, there has been sickness or accident, or there has been some definite reason why the contract has not been fulfilled or the farm paid for before now. It has not been a case of neglect. It has not been a case of carelessness on the part of many of these men who are left there. It has been a case of something over which they have had no control themselves, in almost every instance.
In cases like that, where this number has been reduced to the point at which it stands today, and where the amount represented is only some $1,428,000, I think that we could well consider wiping these debts out now and getting it over with. I think the government would be well advised to do that. It was the opinion of the veterans affairs committee several years ago that we should have done this, but the government did not see fit to adopt that policy. They adopted the policy of dealing with individual cases, and they have been doing a reasonably good job. But in dealing with individual cases, it costs money, it takes time, and there is always the personal angle which comes into it, where the supervisor may like or dislike a particular person; and we find hardship being created where it should not be created. I think that we should give consideration now to this suggestion and I am sure all members of the house would be willing to do so. I see the hon. member for

I hope that the government will take action on it and cancel these few remaining debts.

subtopic: VICTORIA AND JACQUES CARTIER, ST. LAWRENCE RIVER  ABOLITION OF TOLLS
VICTORIA AND JACQUES CARTIER, ST. LAWRENCE RIVER  ABOLITION OF TOLLS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into early consideration the advisability of abolishing the tolls imposed and collected on the Victoria and Jacques Cartier bridges over the St. Lawrence river.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I hope that this motion will not meet the fate of the one that has preceded it. It has been presented to the house on numerous occasions. In fact it was introduced for the first time in 1946, and has appeared on the order paper every year since. In view of the fact that most of the members who may have a greater interest in the motion are from the district of Montreal, and in view of the fact that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier), who is at present in his seat, is also, like the majority in the district of Montreal, of French origin, I am going to deliver my remarks in French.
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, this resolution has appeared many times on the order paper. It does however command the interest of the people I have the honour to represent in the house, and should likewise interest people in all the constituencies on the south shore of the St. Lawrence, and even those of all the ridings of Montreal and of neighbouring towns.
As I indicated just now, I first introduced this motion in 1946, and since then it has appeared each year in my name on the order paper.
This proves that one has to be patient, because the government is not always hasty in relieving evils brought to its attention.
I very sincerely congratulate the new member for St. Mary (Mr. Dupuis) who, a few days ago, in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, praised and commended me for having introduced this notice of motion in the house.
I thank him for his interest in this matter. The problem concerns him perhaps more than any other member for the district of Montreal.

When I heard him say in his maiden speech in this house that he was a keen and true Liberal I understood that since he also supported the motion I had the honour to introduce, he wished in this way to associate himself with those keen Liberals: my colleagues from Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cournoyer) and from St. Johns-Iberville-Napierville (Mr. Alcide Cote). He thus displayed his great devotion and I am sure that he will display it again during the course of his parliamentary career.
I do not intend to speak very long. I already have had the opportunity of introducing this motion and of dealing with it in this house.
As I have already said, this matter comes under both provincial and federal jurisdiction. I would not hold it as a heresy against constitutional law to state that anything concerning roads and their extension, that is to say, bridges, comes under the provincial authorities.
Besides, I am sure that, after what happened recently in Three Rivers, the provincial government realized that the matter was within the realm of their jurisdiction. In this case, however, the federal government certainly has its say, since the two bridges concerned are its property and are operated by its agencies: Jacques Cartier bridge by the national harbours board, and Victoria bridge by the Canadian National Railways.
In moving this resolution, I call upon the house to express the view that the toll should be abolished on these two bridges. I held that view in 1945, I held it before I was elected to the house and I still hold it.
I believe that this toll system is discriminatory. It should be abolished because it requires from one group sacrifices which other groups are not called upon to make. In this case, the tolls on Victoria and Jacques Cartier bridges are detrimental to the whole district on the south shore of the St. Lawrence.
I do not intend to recall one by one the arguments that were brought up, especially in 1947, at the time I discussed the matter. I feel, however, everyone will agree that once a bridge has produced enough to pay its cost the toll should in principle be abolished.
As far as Victoria bridge is concerned, well-informed people know that it was
Tolls on Quebec bridges erected at the turn of the century, with dominion grants. It has always been a toll bridge. It has produced such revenues that it must surely be completely paid for. We also know that the cost of the motor traffic lanes did not exceed $200,000. I was told, on several occasions, that the yearly income derived from the bridge exceeds that amount.
The situation is more difficult as regards Jacques Cartier bridge. It was built in 1930 and was paid for by means of a public loan in the amount of $20 million. At the time the bridge was erected, the interest rate on that loan was' 5 per cent. Therefore the interest charges alone entailed for the nation and the national harbours board, responsible for its administration, an expenditure of over $1 million per year.
It can therefore rightly be claimed, if the interest is taken into account, that Jacques Cartier bridge has, until now, entailed deficits rather than surpluses. Fortunately, and for this I must congratulate the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier), the interest rate was reduced recently when the loan was financed anew on November 1, 1949. I found official confirmation of this information in the annual report of the national harbours board for 1949, from which I quote the following excerpt:
On November 1, 1949, a $19 million bond issue bearing interest at 5 per cent due to mature on November 1, 1969, and put out to cover the cost of building this bridge was recalled, in accordance with the terms of issue, at 105 plus accrued interest. As these bonds could optionally be refunded in United States dollars, steps relating to their withdrawal were taken at the time a Canadian government bond issue went on sale in New York around September 1, 1949.
The Department of Finance advanced the necessary New York funds to the board and the resultant debt was converted into 21 per cent bonds payable in Canadian currency and worth $20,049,750.
I will not read the following lines, for they are of no particular interest at this time.
As a result of the favourable refinancing of the bridge's capital debt, annual interest charges will be reduced by approximately $445,000, interest, exchange (at current rates) and amortization of repurchase costs being taken into account. This reduction of interest charges will enable the bridge to cover its expenses for the first time since its construction.
Therefore, the re-financing of the debt carried out in 1949 had the effect of reducing interest charges by about $500,000 a year. Accordingly, the bridge having probably produced the same revenue, since traffic increases

Toils on Quebec bridges every year, it can be surmised that, tor the first time, the Jacques Cartier bridge surely ended up with a surplus in 1950.
I would have liked to provide the house with official data but the official report has not yet been issued to the general public. Still I believe I may safely state that this year the Jacques Cartier bridge has produced a large surplus.
As far as Victoria bridge is concerned, I have already explained that for a great many years now it has been accumulating surpluses. This, to my mind,. means that these two bridges bring in more than they cost and that there is no more reason to continue to levy tolls on them.
This state of affairs must be brought to as speedy an end as possible. The Canadian National Railways in particular have no good reason to continue levying surplus-producing tolls on Victoria bridge. There is no reason either why the Jacques Cartier bridge should not be made toll-free.
I stated a while ago that these were matters of joint provincial and federal concern.
Consequently it Is impossible to solve this problem without the co-operation of the two administrations concerned. When I was discussing this matter before the house in 1947, the Minister of Transport gave me to understand that he had approached the provincial government for the purpose of settling this problem, one that cannot be settled without the co-operation of the provincial government.
Under a three-way agreement between the provincial government, the federal government and the city of Montreal, no term of the agreement can be changed without the consent of the three parties involved. The federal government must therefore again approach the provincial government. For that reason I call upon the Minister of Transport to take this matter up again with the provincial authorities and seek final settlement of a problem which is a nightmare for my whole county and all residents of the south shore of the St. Lawrence, who have to use that bridge every day.
In the case of Jacques Cartier bridge, the government met with another difficulty. For years the city of Montreal and the provincial government refused to honour the arrange-
[Mr. Pinard.l

ment by which they had agreed to pay their share of the deficit, provided such share did not exceed the sum of $150,000 per year. These amounts were not paid for a few years. Finally the national harbours board sued the city of Montreal and was recently awarded about $700,000. The case now being under appeal and sub judice, I would rather not discuss it further.
There is another matter which I would like to draw to the attention of the house. In a talk that he gave in Montreal and which I had the pleasure of hearing, the Minister of Transport discussed the St. Lawrence waterway project.
In that talk he held out some hope for all who are interested in the matter when he stated that the Lachine section project of the St. Lawrence seaway would lead to settlement of our problem. In this same talk, whose French text I have here in my hand, the Minister of Transport stated that under the Lachine section project a tunnel for railway traffic was to be built below Victoria bridge. Here are the very words the Minister of Transport used on that occasion as he listed the projects involved in the St. Lawrence seaway and gave all the details of the main project itself. In paragraph 4 of a review of those projects he made the following statement:
The plan provides for the construction on the north shore of one or two locks designed to overcome the difference in level and to make navigation possible from Montreal harbour to and above the new industrial area which is to be established. Thus, the level of lake Saint Louis would extend as far as below Victoria bridge and would provide a maximum fall for power development. One of these plans considers diverting railway traffic from Victoria bridge to a tunnel. Thus, Victoria bridge could be used exclusively for motor vehicles. This would improve markedly transportation on the south shore.
As for the project itself, we can judge the reaction of the American press on the discussions now taking place with regard to the St. Lawrence seaway. The project must be approved by the government of the United States before it may be implemented. It is to be hoped that our neighbours will give their approval this year, because Canada has long been awaiting a favourable reply.
Mr. Charles E. Wilson, former president of General Electric, who has been appointed by the American government director of mobilization, came out strongly for this project.

An American senator also stated that, if Mr. Wilson was in favour of that project, he would express a similar opinion. It seems that many people joined hands in an effort to compel the American government, under the leadership of the President, to favour the project. It therefore seems probable that this project will materialize at last, and the hon. Minister of Transport concluded his talk by a sentence that, with his kind permission, I would make my own:
In the interest of national security and our own economy the joint development of power and navigation facilities on the St. Lawrence should be started at once.
I do not claim that the St. Lawrence waterway project should be proceeded with simply to bring about the abolition of tolls on the Victoria and Jacques Cartier bridges. But by this greater achievement the less important problem we are confronted with would be settled.
In closing I beg the hon. Minister of Transport to appeal to the authorities concerned in order that such practices, so unfair to tourists, may finally be abandoned. Indeed tourists find it strange to have to pay 25 cents to be allowed to use an old and dangerous bridge perhaps doomed to the same fate as recently befell another bridge. I want to say that that injustice must be corrected. I therefore urge the Minister of Transport, whose energy and talent are known to all of us, to bring pressure to bear on the government of the province of Quebec, which thus far has been reticent about the matter, so that my electors may be treated fairly and that the people of Quebec may no longer have to pay burdensome tolls on those two bridges.

Mr. Speaker, if I use the French language to speak on this matter, it is because I was not told of this beforehand, and also because, after the brilliant explanation given by the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville (Mr. Pinard), I believe I should speak in my native tongue; besides, it is apparently not lucky for me to use the English language, judging from the experience I had on Monday.
My friend from Chambly-Rouville simply asks that people, wherever they come from, may reach the south shore of the St. Lawrence without having to pay for the privilege. That is right. Naturally Montreal is on the north shore and Arvida also. I can
Tolls on Quebec bridges understand you, Mr. Speaker, preferring it to be that way. But there is an important thing. Those who come from the states, as we say, going through Montreal, and who like to go as far as Riviere-du-Loup, then to Matane, and around the Gaspe peninsula, have to pay a toll to cross the St. Lawrence. Why? Is it because the south shore of the St. Lawrence has become, under a decree issued by my friend the minister, an area of strategical importance. I know that is not his intention. Perhaps if there were only myself, it would be all right; but there are others.
Gaspe is probably the place which the Americans find the most interesting. Why should they be asked an admission fee? Why?
The prime minister of the province of Quebec, Mr. Duplessis, has just announced the discovery of very important mines in the Gaspe peninsula. The Noranda people have already put twelve million dollars into this venture, I am told.
Shall we also have to pay to visit that place? It seems to me unreasonable that we should.
They are turning now to Gaspe because in Abitibi and elsewhere things went wrong. Fortunately, we were assured by Mr. Duplessis and Mr. Gagnon that they would succeed in Gaspe. Praise be to God!
Whether it be Mr. Duplessis, Mr. Onesime
Gagnon or others who develop Gaspe, I take my hat off to them for that district was the first discovered and the last to be recognized.
My friend says people should at least be able to cross the St. Lawrence at Montreal without having to pay. It is because he wants to go to Chambly county. I do the same thing to reach Gaspe, to go to Matane. It is such a rich and beautiful country.
After having thus spoken of the beauty of that district, there is no reason for not visiting that territory where all that wealth has been left, to sleep, alas, for three hundred years. Do not laugh. Go down to Gaspe. Go to Matane, visit the rear concessions, you will see that I am serious.
Thirty years ago they shut the gate; today, Duplessis and others say: Come to Gaspe.
Mr. Speaker, I remember something that happened when I was very young and made me liberal, open-minded. When the Price

If we still have to buy a ticket at the Jacques Cartier bridge or the other bridge to go to the Gaspe peninsula, I really believe we should not be asked to do so. Going down, you know, there are along the shore very nice places; they have surely contributed in a large measure to the development of Canada.
I shall say nothing of Rimouski, but come down and see for yourselves. If it is true that the proposed scheme will further the development of the district, why put up a fence similar to the one the Price Brothers erected thirty years ago? We are told that it will cost 20 cents, 30 cents or 50 cents; I don't know. But why, I ask you?
It is about time that the government should realize what this means. At all events, let the Quebec government build bridges that will not fall down, so that we may have no fear about crossing the river.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to support the motion submitted by the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville (Mr. Pinard). I wish, from the outset to thank him sincerely not so much for praising me as for trusting my word when I said I was a true Liberal. [DOT]
We are considering a motion concerning the Jacques Cartier and Victoria bridges. As the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville pointed out, the matter is not new. For many years we have been calling for the abolition of tolls on those two bridges. Quebec has long resolved that in future there would be no more toll bridges in the province.
Mr. Speaker, I have but very few arguments to submit besides those already put forward by the hon. member. May I draw the attention of the house, however, to two other aspects of the matter. The hon. member could have mentioned them but I thank him for having left this at least to me. It is nothing new but just the same I would like to add them myself to the rightful claims he has expressed so strongly in this house. For many years, the city of Montreal and the


province of Quebec have not ceased paying for the deficits resulting from these two bridges, especially Jacques Cartier bridge.
I believe we should draw the line somewhere. I find it quite unfair that Montreal people should still have to put up with this indirect tax while even on the Quebec bridge, which, I believe, comes under the jurisdiction of the same department, it was found advisable, some years ago, to do away with the toll system.
Why should people in and around Montreal pay this tax when the toll system no longer exists anywhere else in the province?
Let us not forget -that when the bridge was built in 1930, the south shore was not as fully developed and settled as it is now.
Especially since the war, villages and even towns have sprung up there in a few months time. And now the south shore residents, on whose behalf the member for Chambly-Rouville and other members from that part of the province have spoken so well, must cross this bridge daily and even several times a day. Those people are therefore paying more than their fair share of taxation.
I think that to promote the development of the south shore, known as greater Montreal, it is time to abolish this indirect taxation which is proving a burden on those who have to pay it.
I would point out once again that the city of Montreal assumed a substantial burden of debt when the three-way agreement was suggested. In my opinion, it would be easy for the hon. minister, during his talks with the Quebec administration, to reach a new agreement. I have no authority to speak on behalf of the provincial government of Quebec, but it should be possible to reach some new agreement, some new deal by which the province of Quebec would pay part of the deficit on the same basis as the city of Montreal.
I do hope that the very justified request submitted by the hon. member from Chambly-Rouville will be well received by the government and that further talks will be held so as to put an end, as the member from Chambly-Rouville stated, to this discrimination.
There are possibly three or four places in this country where tolls are levied on bridges falling under joint federal and provincial jurisdiction. I hope therefore that the

request made to the government by the hon.
member for Chambly-Rouville will be heard and that we may soon rejoice over the decision taken by the government.
A few years ago I was able to have tolls levied on pedestrians abolished. Originally, when the Jacques Cartier bridge was first opened, pedestrians had to pay five cents for the privilege of crossing the bridge. However, thanks to an agreement between the federal government and the Montreal municipal council, on my request and that of a number of other aldermen at the time, this nuisance was removed.
I bank on the well-known public-spiritedness of the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville and other hon. members to obtain from the government the abolition of that extra tax of toll fees on Jacques Cartier and Victoria bridges.
I will not refer to Victoria bridge in particular, but the injustice there is still more glaring, for that bridge has been paid many times over.
Removal of toll fees on Jacques Cartier bridge would transfer costs to the whole country, but it would be a very moderate cost considering that the bridge is used not only by the people of Montreal but also by people of nearby communities as well as by the tourists who use it all the time.
Under the circumstances I am sure that the government will give sympathetic consideration to our request.
