Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to support the resolution moved by the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville (Mr. Pinard). May I congratulate him upon his interest in the welfare of the people, not only of his county but also of mine and of the eastern townships generally.
He has given a very good outline of the problem and he has distinguished between the two bridges. For my part, I am more interested in the Victoria bridge.
In connection with the Jacques Cartier oridge, my hon. friend has shown what has happened to the request for the abolition of tolls. Everyone knows that a matter of jurisdiction is involved. Everyone knows that the federal government made representations to the provincial authorities with a view to
Tolls on Quebec bridges having the tolls abolished on Jacques Cartier bridge. Unfortunately, as we also know, these offers brought no reply.
For my part, I can understand Mr. Duplessis, the prime minister of the province of Quebec, not being in a mood to discuss bridges now. That might give him nightmares.
I believe that the position of the federal government, which took upon itself the entire cost of building Jacques Cartier bridge, should be made clear to the public. As stated by the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville, certain agreements were made between the provincial government and the city of Montreal on the one hand, and the federal government on the other.
It is not the first time that tolls have been done away with on a bridge built by the federal government. I might mention Quebec bridge as an example. Tolls had been levied on that bridge which was built by the federal government. But under an agreement between the federal and provincial governments tolls were abolished at the same time as they were removed on all other bridges in the province of Quebec.
In the light of that precedent where the case was settled to the satisfaction of all concerned, I submit most respectfully that it would be easy, indeed very easy, for the government of my province to negotiate an agreement with the federal authorities.
On the other hand, I believe the dominion government has exclusive jurisdiction over the levying of the tolls.
Over a period of years, there have been important changes in the rates charged the people who use those bridges. I remember the time when motorists did not have the advantage of buying a booklet of tickets; they just paid 25 cents to get across. Today, they can get books of tickets allowing them to cross at low rates.
On the other hand, I feel the present discrimination should be remedied. It does seem that motorists are paying too high a rate for using the bridge. This is especially hard on merchants who have to deliver goods to Montreal. Then there is the case of dairymen who buy their milk from farmers in the constituencies of Chambly-Rouville and Richelieu-Vercheres and also in the eastern townships. They often pay a toll charge of $1 or $1.50 on their tank trucks. If one con-

Tolls on Quebec bridges siders the number of trucks owned by these people, it is easy to realize what this represents in the way of operating costs.
I do not wish to discuss the matter any longer at present. It would be useless to repeat the reasons so ably stated by my learned friends who spoke before me, but I must say that I heartily endorse their recommendations.

Mr. Speaker, first of all I would like to congratulate my hon. colleague the member from Chambly-Rouville (Mr. Pinard) on the brilliant account he has given the house on this matter.
As a member from the eastern townships, it is my duty to state that this motion has my unqualified support. We of the eastern towrn-ships are particularly concerned with this matter, because we are interested in both bridges, although someone has said that we are concerned only with the Jacques Cartier bridge.
That the people on the south shore have long been the victims of such discrimination is quite true. The hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Coumoyer) stated, a few moments.ago, that tank trucks had to pay toll fees of $1, $1.25 or even $1.50. Let me tell him that he understated the case, for there is in my constituency a co-operative dairy whose tank trucks must pay much more than that for the privilege of crossing that bridge.
Some have mentioned the tourist trade. I really believe that because of the 25 or 40 cents exacted from them, a large number of American tourists cross the bridge leading to Lachine, on their way north, so that they do not come in our district. Ours is a lovely district, yet tolls on Victoria and Jacques Cartier bridges prevent tourists from visiting it. That is unfair to us. Many people from Montreal would spend week ends with us if they did not have that 25 cents to pay. Instead they go north, whereas we have, on the south shore, the finest country in Canada. Furthermore it is even more unfair to the tradesmen on the south shore, who have to pay up to $1 or $1.25 to cross the bridge.
I would ask the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) to try to plead with Mr. Duplessis -even though the latter has been stricken with the bridge disease lately-in order to


convince him to remove that toll. I believe that the Minister of Transport's tact would be equal to the task of convincing the three interested parties to settle the matter, in all fairness to those who live on the south shore and in the eastern townships. And so I ask the Minister of Transport to take the matter up with the authorities as soon as possible so that our people and those from the south shore may obtain justice.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with some caution, in my capacity as member for Three Rivers, that I rise to support the very interesting arguments brought forward by the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville (Mr. Pinard), and by the hon. member for Matapedia-Matane (Mr. Cote). I feel I must bring my humble support and ask the Minister of Transport to kindly accede to the request made by the member for Chambly-Rouville.
In my opinion, the toll system on those bridges is altogether obsolete; it is a source of injustice and hardship for the residents of the various municipalities who have to use them. The population of the -city of Montreal has not always been what it is now. Today, a large number of people working in Montreal have to cross those bridges, two and even four times a day, so that the money spent on tolls amounts to a tidy sum.
It was said a while ago that this matter came under provincial as well as federal jurisdiction. As regards tolls levied on bridges, I think that the provincial government set a good example long ago, since these are the only two toll bridges left in the province of Quebec. I am sure that if the dominion government approached the provincial government on this matter, the latter would maintain the tradition of removing tolls.
That is why it gives me great pleasure to support the request of the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville.
Tourists have also been mentioned. No doubt most of those who visit our province can easily pay the small sum asked of them to cross these two bridges. But I believe that this is a nuisance rather than a real hardship and that such things give our tourist system a bad name. We know that any time

we ourselves must find change to cross a bridge, we cannot help criticizing this system and the government responsible for it.
I sincerely believe that in taking the first steps, the hon. Minister of Transport would, in general, receive really hearty support from the provincial authorities. Such steps would be useful not only to the people of Montreal but also to all the people of the province of Quebec who have to use those bridges. They would also help promote the tourist trade in the province. Let us not forget that this is one of our most profitable industries.
As the member for Three Rivers, on the north shore, I would like toll fees abolished in order that American tourists motoring to the St. Maurice valley and areas north of Montreal can be rid of this nuisance.
As I said a moment ago, the government's persistence in charging toll fees on a bridge as obsolete as the Victoria bridge is rather ridiculous. On Jacques Cartier bridge, a modern and a very sturdy structure, we at least have something to offer. I do feel that tolls on these two bridges should be abolished, that the federal government should shoulder its responsibilities in this matter, and pay for the upkeep of these bridges out of its own treasury instead of pestering the people of Quebec and the public in general.
Mr. Speaker, I see that there are only five minutes left and I would ask you for permission to call it six o'clock.

Being the representative of a constituency which is affected by this deplorable situation, the people in my constituency would expect me, I know, to join with those who have already voiced an opinion on this matter. I am in favour of abolishing the tolls on Jacques Cartier and Victoria bridges. Victoria bridge is the nearest exit for the people of Verdun who wish to cross over to the south shore.
Tolls on Quebec bridges
This matter is very important from both a regional and a national point of view. It is regrettable that, in the most important city of Canada, people should be prevented from coming and going as they wish because of these tolls. There is no reason for it.
I ask the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) and the government to adopt this resolution, for the abolition of those tolls became necessary many years ago, more particularly as far as the toll on Victoria bridge is concerned.
